strengths: Addresses a critical practical problem: the performance degradation gap of 2:4 semi-structured sparsity pruning, which is a real deployment bottleneck for LLMs
Novel and elegant factorization approach (W = A(W'⊙M)B) that provides learned error correction while maintaining hardware compatibility and low overhead (O(N) parameters)
Strong and consistent empirical results across multiple model families (Llama-2, Llama-3, Qwen 2.5, Qwen 3) with ~50% reduction in perplexity gap and substantial improvements on downstream tasks
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple metrics (task accuracy, perplexity on Wikitext2 and C4), proper ablations (block size, selection heuristics), and infrastructure details
Solid theoretical analysis with convergence proofs, including β-smoothness derivations and detailed mathematical foundations
Practical efficiency demonstrated: retains 94-97% of pure 2:4 speedup while achieving better accuracy, enabling real-world deployment
Clear and well-structured presentation with informative figures and thorough appendices covering proofs and implementation details
weaknesses: Theoretical contribution is incremental: Theorem 3.1 only guarantees convergence to initialization (NoWag-P baseline) rather than to an optimal or quality-bounded solution; provides expected monotonic decrease but lacks convergence rate or solution quality guarantees

Computational cost of optimization not analyzed: 20,000 iterations required but wall-clock time not reported; missing runtime comparison with baselines (SparseGPT, Wanda, NoWag-P) which could be critical for practitioners

Block size hyperparameter selection lacks principled approach: Figure 3 shows exponential sensitivity but dblock=128 fixed across all models; no systematic justification or guidance for choosing block size for different model sizes

Hardware efficiency claims need refinement: stated as 'majority of speedups retained' but actually 94-97% (Table 4), with absolute speedup loss non-negligible at scale (e.g., 1.041x vs 1.071x for 14B model)

Limited novelty in algorithmic components beyond the factorization: block coordinate descent is standard, greedy enumeration of 6 masks is straightforward, resembles existing low-rank approximation techniques

Insufficient analysis of learned representations: minimal insight into what A and B matrices learn or why factorization helps particularly for reasoning tasks; no visualization or detailed interpretation

Missing experimental comparisons: criticizes DSF as incompatible with 2:4 sparsity but provides no empirical comparison; limited comparison with other decomposition-based or low-rank pruning approaches
Scalability and memory overhead concerns: largest models tested are 70-72B; ARMOR uses more VRAM than pure 2:4 sparsity (28.11GB vs 27.52GB for 7B); O(N) overhead impact unclear at 100B+ scale

Proxy loss surrogate objective may be limiting: optimizes data-aware but still layer-wise NoWag loss; correlation between proxy loss and final performance only shown on Llama-2-7B/C4; potential misalignment not thoroughly explored

Reproducibility limitations: code stated as 'currently being prepared' and unavailable at review time; transition from theoretical sequential GD to practical joint Adam optimization lacks full justification

strengths: Novel matrix factorization approach using block-diagonal wrappers around sparse cores, elegantly motivated and technically sound
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple model families (Qwen, Llama) with consistent, substantial improvements (~50% perplexity gap reduction on Llama-2-13B)
Dual evaluation strategy combining downstream tasks (7 benchmarks) and perplexity metrics, demonstrating broad applicability
Rigorous convergence proof with proper beta-smoothness analysis and detailed mathematical treatment
Thorough ablation studies examining block size, selection heuristics, and calibration data robustness
Strong reproducibility commitment with promised code release, detailed implementation specifications, and clear hyperparameter documentation
Demonstrated practical efficiency retention despite optimization overhead, achieving ~84% of theoretical speedup in unoptimized PoC
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: combines well-established techniques (block coordinate descent, gradient descent, greedy mask selection) without fundamental innovation
Weak theoretical contribution: Theorem 3.1 only guarantees reaching initialization quality (NoWag-P level), with empirical gains unexplained by theoretical results
Computational overhead insufficiently addressed: 20,000 optimization iterations required but wall-clock time not reported; 'one-shot' claim is misleading
Speedup-accuracy trade-off understated: practical speedup reduced from 1.217× to 1.141× with 3.4% FLOP overhead and increased model size (9.25GB vs 8.89GB); practical benefit questioned
Hardware implementation gap unresolved: only PyTorch PoC evaluated; no native 2:4 sparse kernel implementation or production hardware deployment path
Critical hyperparameter block size (dblock=128) fixed across all models despite high sensitivity shown in Figure 3; no principled selection guidance provided
Limited comparison with learnable baselines: MaskLLM dismissed without empirical comparison; DenoiseRotator results mixed; comparisons incomplete
MoE evaluation underdeveloped: single model with non-standard settings (1,000 iterations) and limited baseline comparisons
Weak initialization analysis: convergence depends on NoWag-P initialization, robustness to alternatives not explored
Greedy sparse core update is heuristic with no optimality guarantees or local optimality analysis; limitations not discussed

strengths: Novel and well-motivated factorization approach (W = A(W'⊙M)B) that shifts pruning from weight removal to representation learning; elegant use of block-diagonal wrappers as learned error correctors

Exceptionally strong and consistent empirical results across 12+ model configurations; ~50% reduction in perplexity gap (Llama-2-13B: 8.28→6.37), outperforms multiple SOTA baselines (SparseGPT, Wanda, NoWag-P) on both perplexity and diverse downstream tasks

Practical hardware efficiency: retains majority of 2:4 speedup (~84% of 2x theoretical on unoptimized code) with only ~3.4% flop overhead; maintains memory benefits with tunable accuracy-latency trade-off
Solid theoretical foundation with convergence proof (Theorem 3.1), convexity and β-smoothness analysis, though modest in scope

Technical ingenuity in exploiting 2:4 structure (6 possible masks) enabling efficient parallel optimization of ~10³ blocks; closed-form least squares solutions with clever gradient-weighted random sampling

Comprehensive experimental validation: extensive ablations (selection heuristics, calibration data, block size), comparisons with concurrent methods, extensions to N:M/unstructured/MoE, good reproducibility details
Clear presentation with intuitive figures, well-organized appendices with complete proofs and implementation details
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: theory uses sequential gradient descent with computed β-smoothness learning rates; practice uses joint Adam with fixed 10⁻⁴ learning rate. No analysis of impact on convergence or solution quality

Convergence guarantee is modest: Theorem 3.1 only guarantees monotonic decrease to local optimum (potentially suboptimal); bound L_t ≤ L_0 is weak, essentially avoiding regression from NoWag-P initialization which determines initial value

Incomplete baseline comparisons: DenoiseRotator results mixed (competitive but not consistently better), comparisons at different sequence lengths complicate interpretation, MaskLLM and some low-rank methods excluded

Optimization algorithm complexity with many hyperparameters (block size, learning rate, 20K iterations, L1 vs. L2 gradient weighting). Gradient weighting choice lacks strong justification; ablation shows only marginal gains (~1-2%, Table 7)

Limited insight into when/why ARMOR helps: largest gains on reasoning tasks without mechanistic explanation; no per-layer analysis; no investigation of learned A,B structure. Block size ablation lacks explanation for diminishing returns

Experimental limitations: tiny calibration set (128 samples, 500K-1M tokens)—robustness is good but unexplained; MoE experiments limited (1K vs 20K iterations); single-GPU inference; no pruning+quantization evaluation despite orthogonality claim
Circular initialization logic: initialization exactly matches NoWag-P solution, making guarantee that ARMOR ≥ NoWag-P somewhat tautological. Alternative initializations not explored

Pruning computational cost not quantified; design choices (L1 norm, block-diagonal structure) lack justification; wall-clock compression time unreported; redacted GitHub link limits reproducibility verification
